Three Rules for Great Web Design Building a great website can be an intimidating task. With so many websites out there, how do you make sure yours gets noticed? Many web designers feel pressure to make their website unique, but being too unique can be a recipe for failure. It turns out that most successful websites share some common characteristics. So the challenge of successful web design is not to come up with a totally new design, but rather to identify the features that make a website successful and make sure they are in your design. As John D Rockefeller once said, "The secret to success is to do the common thing uncommonly well." In this post we'll examine what makes a great website. The 3 Click Rule One common characteristic of most successful websites is that they are easy to navigate. Users don't want to spend a lot of time navigating your site. They want to get where they need to go – fast. The more time a user has to spend on your site trying to find what they are looking for, the more likely they are to leave your site. In general, it should take a user no more than 3 clicks to do anything. Whether they are trying to buy a product, contact customer support, or post a review, make sure users can accomplish it in no more than 3 clicks. Less is More Many web designers feel pressure to make the most of their website's home page. That can be a mistake. A home page that is too crowded with information can chase users away from your site. Identify the information that is most essential to your website. Put that on your home page – and nothing else. Do the expected Most good websites put certain features in the same basic places. The link to the user's shopping cart is almost always in the upper-right-hand corner. Links to social media are generally in the bottom left. When important features like these are not in the places users expect them to be, users get frustrated and will leave your site. Don't move away from these standard practices

EVOLVE LEVEL 5, Unit Quiz 1 1A Alex: Hi, Sally. Do you have a moment? Sally: Sure, Alex. What's up? Alex: Well, I'm a little worried about something I heard. About a possible office move … ? Sally: Yeah, I heard something about it too. But that's just a rumor, Alex. I don't think you should worry about something that might never happen. Alex: I don't know … I heard it from Mr. Miller, from accounting, so it's from a trustworthy source. I don't believe Mr. Miller would ever make up a story like that. Sally: Hmm … You're right. He's not someone who would be spreading false information around. And he would probably be informed about something like that before we were. But when did Mr. Miller tell you about that? Alex: Yesterday. We went out for lunch, and I asked him whether the office would be redecorated this summer. Sally: You didn't! Alex: I did … You know how these redecorations can sometimes cause a lot of trouble. But then he told me that it would probably not be necessary because we might be moving! Sally: Oh boy … Did he say when? Alex: Not really. He just suggested that it might not happen anytime soon. But from a few things he said, it sounded like it could happen before the end of the year. Sally: That is soon. Alex: Yes! And what really worries me is that the office might be moved further from downtown. That would make life so difficult – long commuting to work, not having time to take the children to school, getting home late. It will be a nightmare. Sally: Come on, Alex. We don't even know for sure if or when it might happen. So, before we start worrying, I think we need to find someone who could give us a more accurate report of what is going on …

Imperfect goods  I recently purchased a pair of fishing boots from your website. At first, I was hesitant as I've had bad experiences ordering fishing gear online in the past. I'm a serious fisherman, and my fishing equipment gets used pretty heavily. So I didn't want to buy anything cheap or second-rate and was willing to spend good money on a quality product. I read the online reviews of the boots. They were all very enthusiastic, and this is what convinced me to finally buy them. Unfortunately, those reviews have not turned out to be trustworthy. Basically, everything in those reviews or in your advertisements has turned out to either be misleading or completely untrue. First, the photos on your website show that the boots go above the knee, which is important when you're wading in a foot or two of water. The boots I received barely go halfway up my calf. So while they are technically waterproof, that's only true as long as you are standing in no more than a few inches of water. The lining of the boots was another disappointment. I read review after review talking about how warm and comfortable the lining was. That was certainly true at the start. The first couple of times I wore the boots they felt great. But the lining quickly started to come apart. I'm honestly shocked that you would use such inferior materials. Really, about the only part of the online reviews that was accurate was all the praise for the delivery service. Delivery was fast and on time, but given all the problems with these boots, that doesn't really matter. I know that your website clearly states that you do not accept returns, but I hope that you will make an exception to that policy and provide me with a full refund. I think it would also be helpful if you corrected some of the misleading information on your website so that customers had a better idea of what they are actually buying. Sincerely, Dave Curtis

Urban legends What are urban legends? They are unproven, hard-to-believe stories, which are generally told as if they are true. In this way, urban legends are similar to superstitions and folklore. A major difference, however, is that urban legends tend to be specific to a nation or a specific generation – the urban legends known to a 20-year-old in Brazil would likely be very different to the urban legends known to a 40-year-old in Spain. So, how do urban legends start? Urban legends often start with some element of truth, but as the story is told and retold, the details get more and more exaggerated. Also, as the story is told again and again, it becomes a part of the culture of a country or community. One surprising thing about urban legends is how enduring they are. In the modern internet age, most urban legends are easily disproven. For example, a widely-spread urban legend in the United States claims that if a tooth is left in a cup of soda overnight, the soda will completely dissolve the tooth. This is easily disproven with a quick internet search, and yet this urban legend is still being told as if it were true. In fact, if anything, the internet seems to be making it easier for urban legends to spread. There seem to be two main factors driving the spread of urban legends in the digital age. The first is the ease and speed with which information spreads. In previous eras, urban legends were largely spread by word-of-mouth, with one person directly telling another. Urban legends were rarely spread through media because traditional publishers, such as newspapers and magazines, were concerned with the accuracy of the information they published. In the digital age, anyone can publish information to a wide audience, meaning that misinformation spreads much more quickly. The other main factor is human nature. Most people love to tell a good story, even if it's too good to be true

Host: And today we have the pleasure of talking to Oscar Suarez, an exceptionally talented and imaginative young designer who has really brightened up the final day of this season's Fashion Week. Welcome to our show, Oscar. Oscar: Thank you for inviting me. Host: Oscar, I understand that you don't consider yourself a "designer". Could you explain that better to our listeners? Oscar: Well, I like to think of myself as a "creator." I create things; I don't only "design" them. Of course, lately, I have been mainly designing clothes, accessories, shoes. However, in the past, I also created home decorations and even furniture. And I have also worked as an illustrator. I've done illustrations for magazines, books, and even for packaging. Host: Oh, I was not aware of your work as an illustrator. Oscar: Yes, not many people know about it. And I sometimes create sculptures as well, although I don't consider myself particularly competent at that. Host: Wow! I think you definitely deserve to be called a "creator." Now … how did this brilliant career as a creator start? Oscar: Uh … I was already pretty artistic as a child. However, I think that what really set me on this career path was a vacation in Madrid with my grandparents when I was thirteen. We visited the Prado Museum, and some of the works of art I saw there really captured my imagination and left a lasting impression on me. On that trip, I realized that I really wanted to create beautiful things that would raise people's spirits and brighten up their days. Host: So, it was very fortunate for us that your grandparents decided to take you to the Prado. Oscar: Ha. I would say that it was especially fortunate for me to have such fantastic grandparents. They have always encouraged me to improve my skills, to learn more about art and design. They have also always supported my decision to have a career associated with the arts. I sometimes think they considered me … I don't know … gifted. Host: You certainly are extremely talented. Now, what about your parents? Have they also encouraged you to pursue a more artistic career? Oscar: Well, they have never prevented me from having one, but they have always had doubts about whether this was the best path for me. Host: Interesting … Now … you went to college in Boston, correct?

How to measure success Success means different things to different people. Here are some words of wisdom about how to measure the success in your life. A Decide what really matters to you. It is common to think of success as something concrete, such as having a well-paid job. But it's important to make a list of different success factors which include material and non-material things, such as emotional well-being, personal satisfaction, friendships. B Compare yourself only against yourself and not others. We often measure our success by comparing ourselves to others. By doing so, we are being unfair to ourselves, often setting unreachable goals which can be a real downer. So, a word of advice, chart your own progress towards that goal, and remember to congratulate yourself when you can see that progress is being made. C Measure things which are not normally measured. Some things like wealth are easy to measure. You look at your bank statement and you can see the amount of money that you have. But there are many other areas of life which we can evaluate and measure which are not so obviously countable. For example, if you decide that success for you is about feeling confident, then this can be measured by observing how confident you feel every day. D Be patient. Think about the long-term goals. Real success is not something that is usually obtained overnight. Financial stability is not often found by winning the lottery, nor is true love often found in an instant. In order to get genuine stability, both financial and emotional, it might take time, so you need to be determined and patient. E Re-evaluate if what you wanted yesterday is still the same today. The search for success is a journey and some journeys take longer than others. So you may need to go back to step 1 from time to time to re-evaluate what really matters and how relevant that is today

Moderator: Today, our debate teams will be discussing whether our personalities are more influenced by nature or nurture. Is our behavior and the way we think mainly shaped by the genes we receive from our parents? Or do environmental factors, such as the place where we live and the people we live with, influence our personalities more? So, please welcome Miranda and Derek, who are going to be discussing the topic and giving us their opinion. Miranda, could we start with your point of view? Miranda: I strongly believe that we are who we are due to nature. I don't deny that our environment can also have a powerful effect on how we think and behave, but I firmly believe that genetics plays a much more important role on our personality. Take my family, for example. All my grandparents were musicians, and both my parents ended up being exceptionally musical. They both started their careers as concert pianists at a very early age. And, although my sister and I are not as talented as our parents, we have also played an instrument since we were young children. People may argue that our grandparents encouraged our parents to study music, and that they, in turn, encouraged us to do the same – which would explain why our family is so good at playing music. However, that would not explain why some of us were so talented at such an early age. I do believe that the existence of people exceptionally gifted at something from an early age demonstrates that nature is the main influence on our personality, our views on life and our behavior. Moderator: Thank you for your views, Miranda. Derek, do you agree with Miranda? Derek: I'm afraid that I don't entirely agree with Miranda's views. My opinion is that people can also become extremely good at something simply by studying and practicing. They don't need to be born that way. If your parents encouraged you to study music from an early age and you devoted enough hours to practice, there is no reason why you wouldn't become an exceptionally skilled musician too. Miranda: I agree that people can learn to be highly competent at most things through practice. However, there is a difference between being competent and being talented. And I don't believe you can learn to be talented. Derek: I think that the difference is very subjective

Presentation nerves? Knowing how to give a successful presentation and to be a competent public speaker is a very useful life skill to have. Before the Presentation A Think about the core message. Ask yourself what you want your audience to remember at the end of the talk. Once you know this, you'll know what you need to say. B Know your audience. If you understand the needs of your audience you'll be able to write a talk which suits their particular needs. So, do some homework and find out a bit about the profile of your audience before you start. C Be prepared. Make some cards with the key messages on to help you remember what you want to say. Practice at home or in front of friends before the big day. During the presentation D Limit the slides. Slides are there to add visual support to your argument and to capture the imagination of your audience. However, you shouldn't depend on them too much. The most important thing you have is your voice. E Keep it simple. Keep the text to a minimum and remember the quality not the quantity of what you say is the most important. F Create expectation. Remember that you are taking your audience on a journey. So, create expectation at the beginning through images, music, anecdotes, or humor. Expectation gives your audience a reason to listen to you. G Have a strong beginning and end. It's important to start and end with something memorable. These are the parts that are key and that leave a lasting impression on people. H Don't be afraid of making mistakes. Even the most trained speakers make mistakes, so if you do, don't let it ruin your day. I Be enthusiastic. Your enthusiasm will make you sound convincing and will raise the audience's spirits. J Relax and remember to breathe! Giving a presentation shouldn't stress you out. Enjoy giving the talk and your audience will too
